home.title: GPU Unlock — build, install and verify the SM speed-select modules
home.description: A project hub for the NVIDIA SM speed-select override kernel modules: pick the module for your card, build it, wire it into the initramfs, opt in on the kernel command line and verify the result.
home.h1: Install the SM speed-select override, module by module
home.lead: Three kernel modules unlock the tensor throughput NVIDIA reserves for other parts of the chip. This site is the build-and-install side of the project: which module your card needs, the exact commands, the parameter names and the checks that prove it worked. Which cards are supported and what was measured on them is recorded separately on the reference site.
home.modulesIntro: Two of the three share the module name gpu_unlock; the Turing one is a different module with a different parameter. Install the one your chip belongs to — the wrong parameter does nothing at all, silently.
home.quickstartBody: None of the modules ships prebuilt binaries. Each one builds on the target machine, because the payload is generated against the NVIDIA firmware already installed there. The same make install front end covers every distribution family.
home.optInTitle: Opt in on the kernel command line
home.optInBody: A module that loads but is not asked to do anything leaves the card locked. The parameter is the switch, and it has to survive into the boot entry.
home.verifyTitle: Verify before you make it permanent
home.verifyBody: The unlock is invisible when it fails, so check each step rather than assuming.
home.verify1: Boot once with the parameter in place and watch the kernel log for the unlock line
home.verify2: Confirm the card is in the accepted device-ID list for your module
home.verify3: Re-measure a path that the override is supposed to change, on the same card
home.riskTitle: The hardware risk is documented, not theoretical
home.riskBody: The modules write speed-select registers and perform an FLR before the driver binds. Keep an unmodified stock boot entry, validate one cold boot before making anything persistent, and treat the AD103 path as experimental — it was validated on a single card.
home.referenceTitle: Card support and measured results live on the reference site
home.referenceBody: Supported device IDs, per-card status and the same-card stock-vs-unlocked measurements are maintained on the companion reference site, which is where the evidence lives. This site covers the build, the boot order and the checks.
home.upstreamBody: This site documents these repositories; it does not fork them.
home.upstreamUsage: this project's own usage notes and install walkthrough

modules.ampere: The original module: GA102, GA103, GA104 and GA106, loaded as gpu_unlock.
modules.ada: The Ada fork: adds AD102 and an experimental AD103 canary, and still covers the Ampere lists.
modules.turing: A separate module for RTX 20 series cards, loaded as turing_unlock with its own parameter.

gpus.title: Supported NVIDIA cards
gpus.description: The PCI IDs the GPU Unlock module accepts, split by how well each one is actually known: measured on the same card, reported by a user, partial, untested, or deliberately unsupported.
gpus.summary: {total} PCI IDs accepted across the Ampere, Ada and Turing modules (AD102, AD103, GA102, GA103, GA104, GA106, TU102, TU104, TU106); {cards} cards described here.

statusExplain.measured: A fork published stock-vs-unlocked numbers from one card with the same binaries.
statusExplain.reported: Someone filed a compatibility report. The forks did not independently revalidate it.
statusExplain.partial: The override applies but tensor throughput stays where it was.
statusExplain.untested: The module accepts the device ID. Nobody has published a result.
statusExplain.unsupported: Deliberately not in the accepted list.

gpus.idsTitle: How to check your own card
gpus.idsBody: Run `lspci -nn | grep -i nvidia` and match the `10de:xxxx` device ID against the list above. GeForce and CMP GA102/GA104 IDs are in the Ampere/Ada list; professional RTX A-series and data-centre parts are not. AD102 accepts only the RTX 4090, and AD103 is limited to the exact RTX 4070 Ti SUPER canary address. On RTX 20 series cards the accepting module is `turing_unlock`, and AD102/GA102 IDs mean nothing to it.

device.benchNote: Same card, same binary, stock versus unlocked. Modes that did not change are reported too — an unlock that does not move a path is a fact worth having.
device.noBench: No same-card measurement has been published for this card. Its status comes from user compatibility reports, not from a benchmark run under the maintainers' control.

bench.title: Benchmarks: stock versus unlocked
bench.description: Every same-card stock-vs-unlocked measurement published upstream, including the tensor modes that did not change, the FP8 CUTLASS pair that measured 1.0029×, and the RTX 2080 Ti cuBLAS table from the Turing fork.
bench.methodBody: The RTX 4090 rows come from a register-resident MMA issue-rate loop run at 20,000 iterations and three repetitions per mode, best-of-three reported. The RTX 4070 Ti SUPER rows come from the fork's tensor-modes-comparison.json, 66 SMs, driver 580.178.04, 240 W cap, 20,000 iterations and three repetitions, with all-one inputs across eight independent chains. The FP8 pair is a separate CUTLASS 4.8.1 profiler run on one sm_89 kernel. The RTX 2080 Ti rows are the Turing fork's README table: cuBLAS FP16 GEMM with FP32 accumulate, 250 W, driver 575.51.03, four M.N.K sizes, measured on a Dell 22 GB card. The README states TFLOPS directly and gives percent of a 56.9 TF/s peak in parentheses, which the author takes from the NVIDIA Turing whitepaper; those TFLOPS are quoted here unchanged. The README gives no iteration count, so none is shown.
bench.fp8Title: The FP8 pair that did not move
bench.fp8Body: The fork measured a matched E4M3 FP8 input, FP32 accumulate 4096³ GEMM on the 4070 Ti SUPER with the same CUTLASS profiler binary, one kernel, 10 warmups and 20 profiling iterations, requiring device-reference verification. Both runs passed their reference checks.
bench.readTitle: How to read a ratio of 1.00×
bench.readBody: A 1.00× row is not a failed unlock. It says that particular path was never rate-limited, so the override had nothing to restore. If you benchmark your own card and see 1.00× on the mode you care about, the unlock may well have applied correctly and simply does not help that workload.

install.title: Install GPU Unlock
install.description: The install order that matters: build locally, let the package put the right module (gpu_unlock or turing_unlock) in the initramfs before nvidia, opt in on the kernel command line, and only then make the boot entry persistent.
install.riskBody: The module writes speed-select registers and performs an FLR before the NVIDIA driver binds. Keep a stock boot entry. Validate a cold boot before making anything persistent. The AD103 path is experimental and was validated on one card. The Turing flow does the same, and its README warns that tensor cores draw very high power and that unlocking them may damage your hardware.
install.verifyBody: The module logs its decisions to the kernel ring buffer. Check the log and confirm the driver bound the card afterwards.
install.disableBody: Remove gpu_unlock.targets= from the kernel command line for Ampere/Ada, or turing_unlock.targets= for the RTX 20 series; for a one-off boot, delete it in the bootloader's edit screen. Removing the packages also removes the module and the initramfs drop-ins.
install.repoAmpere: Ampere: GA102, GA103, GA104, GA106. No Ada support.
install.repoAda: Ada: adds AD102 RTX 4090 and the experimental AD103 canary, and keeps the Ampere device list.
install.repoTuring: Turing: the RTX 20 series (TU102, TU104, TU106) via a separate module, turing_unlock. Ampere/Ada modules do not touch these cards.

requirements.linux-headers: Linux with kernel headers and a working DKMS toolchain (all three forks).
requirements.source-build: GPL-2.0-only source built locally — the pinned NVIDIA firmware is downloaded and generated on your own machine.
requirements.stock-entry: An unmodified stock boot entry kept available, so a failed unlock is recoverable.
requirements.accepted-pci-id: A card whose PCI ID is in the module's accepted list (see the cards index).

pick-fork.title: Pick the fork that matches your card
pick-fork.body: The Ampere fork (Zagitta/gpu-unlock, v1.0.0) covers GA102, GA103, GA104 and GA106. The Ada fork (JustAResearcher/gpu-unlock-ada, v1.1.1) is that same module with AD102 (RTX 4090) and an experimental AD103 canary added, so it also handles the Ampere device list. The Turing fork (nlzy/turing-unlock, v2.0.0) is a separate module for the RTX 20 series: TU102, TU104 and TU106.
pick-fork.note: The Ada fork keeps the original GeForce/CMP GA102 and GA104 lists plus the newer GA103/GA106 list. Professional RTX A-series and data-centre parts are not accepted by any of them. Turing and Ampere/Ada modules are not interchangeable — a TU102 card will not be touched by `gpu_unlock`.

clone.title: Clone and build the packages locally
clone.body: None of the three forks ships prebuilt binaries: each builds on the target machine, because the firmware generation step is pinned to the NVIDIA firmware you already have installed.
clone.note: All three forks use the same `make install` front end, which detects the distribution family. Explicit targets are `make install-arch`, `make install-deb` and `make install-rpm`. Kernel headers and a DKMS toolchain must already be present. The Turing build downloads two pinned NVIDIA files and verifies their SHA-256 — they stay in `~/.cache/turing-unlock/inputs`, and `make inputs` fetches them ahead of time.

initramfs.title: Let the package wire the module into the initramfs
initramfs.body: The unlock only applies if the module loads before the NVIDIA driver binds the card — `gpu_unlock` on Ampere/Ada, `turing_unlock` on the RTX 20 series. Loading it manually afterwards cannot unlock it, because the module refuses a card that already has a driver bound (`-EBUSY`). Each package therefore puts its module and firmware into the initramfs and loads it there.
initramfs.note: With initramfs-tools and dracut the module is rebuilt for every installed kernel that has headers, and images are rebuilt on install and on removal. Kernels installed later get the module from their own install hooks. mkinitcpio ignores drop-ins for an image built with `-c <config>` or a preset `_config` — put `gpu_unlock` (or `turing_unlock`) right before `nvidia` in that config's MODULES yourself.

opt-in.title: Opt in on the kernel command line
opt-in.body: The module does nothing unless the kernel command line asks for it. Set `gpu_unlock.targets=` to `all` for the Ampere path, or to explicit PCI addresses.
opt-in.note: There is no `softdep nvidia pre:` rule on purpose: kmod honours only the first `softdep nvidia` line it reads, so another package's rule would silently win. Boot order is handled by the initramfs drop-in instead.

turing-opt-in.title: Turing uses a different parameter name
turing-opt-in.body: The RTX 20 series module is `turing_unlock`, so the option is `turing_unlock.targets=` — not `gpu_unlock.targets=`. It accepts `all` or a comma-separated list of PCI addresses printed by `lspci -D`; case does not matter. Without the option the module loads and returns without touching anything.
turing-opt-in.note: Targets are matched by PCI address, and the module serialises cards behind one mutex, so they are unlocked one at a time. If a driver already owns the card, the module leaves it alone and logs `unlock failed (-16)` (EBUSY) — that is a load-order problem, not a card problem. The module does a PCIe FLR first if the card state needs it. On success the card is not reset; a failed step may reset it, and the screen then stays blank until `nvidia-drm` takes over.

ad103.title: AD103 needs two opt-ins and one exact address
ad103.body: RTX 4070 Ti SUPER (`10de:2705`) is experimental and validated on a single card. It requires both `gpu_unlock.ad103_experimental=1` and `gpu_unlock.targets=` set to that card's single exact PCI address. `targets=all` never selects it.
ad103.note: Other Ada IDs, professional A-series and data-centre parts are not accepted. Shared firmware across Ada chips does not establish support for untested cards.

resume.title: Know what happens across suspend
resume.body: This applies to `gpu_unlock` (Ampere/Ada) only: it reapplies the override on resume, which can reset a display card. Add `gpu_unlock.resume=0` to the kernel command line — or write `0` to `/sys/module/gpu_unlock/parameters/resume` — to turn that off. Hibernation is not covered either way.
resume.note: `turing_unlock` has no resume parameter and no resume hook; it runs once from the initramfs and has no module parameters besides `targets`.

make-persistent.title: Persist the boot entry only after a cold boot works
make-persistent.body: Validate one cold boot and one warm reboot on the exact card first. Only then make the bootloader entry persistent. Keep an unmodified stock entry available, and re-verify `gpu_unlock: unlocked`, the rate readback and GPU health after each boot.
make-persistent.note: The tested canary uses a kernel-version-specific image; regenerate and revalidate it before removing its pinned kernel during an upgrade.

avoid.title: Do not let the driver load early
avoid.body: Avoid `nvidia-smi`, CUDA, NVML and `nvidia-modprobe` before a manual cold-card attempt: they can load NVIDIA by name, and ordinary modprobe blacklist rules do not block explicit named loads. The packaged initramfs flow avoids the need for manual firmware staging.

tensor-unchanged.symptom: Card stays unlocked but tensor throughput is unchanged
tensor-unchanged.cause: Some cards complete the unlock without gaining the rate (RTX 3080 Ti 20 GB OEM reports BF16 staying at half rate). Verify with a same-card stock-vs-unlocked benchmark rather than assuming the unlock implies the speedup.

blank-display.symptom: Display stays blank after the unlock
blank-display.cause: Expected during handoff: the firmware framebuffer is removed just before FLR and the display stays blank until `nvidia-drm` takes over. Display handoff was not part of the RTX 4090 validation.

unlocked-log-only.symptom: `gpu_unlock` appears in the log but the card is not unlocked
unlocked-log-only.cause: The module loaded after NVIDIA had already bound the card, or `gpu_unlock.targets=` is missing/wrong. The override must run from the initramfs, before the driver binds.

turing-silent.symptom: `turing_unlock` logs nothing at all on an RTX 20 card
turing-silent.cause: `turing_unlock.targets=` is missing, so the module returned immediately: it does nothing without the option. Using `gpu_unlock.targets=` instead produces exactly this silence, because the Ampere/Ada module never touches TU102/TU104/TU106.

turing-ebusy.cause: EBUSY: a driver had already bound the card when the module ran. The unlock must happen from the initramfs, before `nvidia` binds; check that the package's initramfs drop-in is present and that the image was rebuilt.

turing-unlock-failed.cause: The module logs the error code and leaves the card alone. A failed step may reset the card, which blanks the display until `nvidia-drm` loads. If the GPU firmware does not stop, the module keeps its DMA buffers until the next power off — power off before retrying.

firmware-never-stops.symptom: Firmware on a card never stops
firmware-never-stops.cause: The module logs it and keeps the DMA buffers that firmware may still use until the next power off. Power off before trying again.

faq.title: GPU Unlock module FAQ
faq.description: How the three modules differ, which one a given card needs, how the initramfs load order works, and what to do when the unlock silently does nothing.
faq.a1: RTX 30 series cards use the Ampere module. RTX 40 series cards use the Ada fork, which also keeps the Ampere device list. RTX 20 series cards use the Turing module, which is a separate kernel module with a separate parameter. The card list and the accepted PCI IDs live on gpuunlock.com.
faq.q2: Can I use one module for everything?
faq.a2: No. The Ada fork covers Ampere and Ada, so one clone is enough for RTX 30 and 40 series cards. The Turing module shares no code with it and has to be installed alongside if you have both a 20 series and a 30 or 40 series card.
faq.q3: Why does the module have to load before the NVIDIA driver?
faq.a3: The override has to happen before the driver binds the card. The driver writes the locked speed-select state during its own probe, so a module loaded afterwards has nothing left to change. The package therefore drops the module into the initramfs, which runs before the driver is even installed.
faq.q4: The unlock did nothing, what should I check first?
faq.a4: Check the kernel ring buffer for the module's own log line. If the module never logged, the initramfs drop-in is missing or the parameter did not reach the kernel command line. If it logged that the card was skipped, the PCI ID is not in the module's accepted list.
faq.a5: Yes. Remove the opt-in parameter from the kernel command line and the module stops touching the card. The kernel parameter is what selects the card, so the same mechanism is both the opt-in and the opt-out.
faq.q6: Does the Turing module work the same way?
faq.a6: Same principle, different names: turing_unlock.targets= instead of gpu_unlock.targets=, and turing_unlock instead of gpu_unlock in the initramfs. Copying an Ampere command onto a 20 series card is the most common way to waste a boot cycle.

windows.title: GPU Unlock on Windows
windows.description: The Windows route from impacifist/Windows-GPU-UNLOCK: a UEFI application unlocks the card and chain-loads the Windows Boot Manager, so the card stays unlocked under the stock NVIDIA driver without rebooting into Linux.
windows.lead: The Linux module on this site has to load before the NVIDIA driver, which means a reboot into Linux. This project goes the other way: a self-built UEFI application does the same register write, then hands control to the Windows Boot Manager in the same boot. The card comes up unlocked under the stock Windows driver.
windows.packageBody: This site builds a setup program from the pinned v{version} source archive. It installs the scripts, the documentation and the licences as a plain source drop — nothing is prebuilt, because the EFI image has to be compiled against your own partitions. Firmware dumps and driver DLLs are not included and cannot be, so the installer is a shortcut for the checkout, not for the unlock.
windows.packageNote: Unsigned and unofficial: it is not published by NVIDIA, ASUS or impacifist. Windows will warn about an unknown publisher. Verify the SHA-256 of the archive before running the scripts, and read the compatibility page before building — a successful build is not a permission to unlock.
windows.routesIntro: Same EFI payload, three ways to get it in front of Windows. Pick one; they are not steps in a sequence. All commands are copied verbatim from the pinned documentation.

source.b: Clone the v{version} tag rather than the default branch. The documentation and the EFI build are tied to that revision, and the local files the scripts write are not portable between revisions.

usb.b: An ordinary FAT32 stick; no partition is created, resized or retyped and no firmware boot entry is registered. The tool validates the five asset sizes and hashes and writes a new local folder — copy its contents to the stick root yourself.

internal.b: A separate GPT FAT32 EFI System Partition of at least 1 GiB, prepared by hand after a backup. Configure.ps1 writes ignored local files; Build.ps1 compiles a wrapper and a child with a hash contract. Neither changes boot settings.

headless.b: Staging alone changes no boot entry, boot order or Fast Startup. -Register appends a separate F8 entry and keeps the existing boot priority. The documented boot is F8 → GPU Headless UNLOCK, with no key presses after that.

restore.b: One documented command puts Windows first again. Keep the local state and backups the scripts write: they are recovery inputs, not release files.

windows.assetsTitle: Five firmware files you must supply
windows.assetsBody: The packaging tool and the UEFI application both reject mismatched hashes, so similar versions cannot be substituted. Generate them from legally obtained NVIDIA inputs with the pinned upstream pipeline; the site links the procedure rather than the files.
windows.assetsNote: Not redistributed here or in the installer: NVIDIA firmware, VBIOS/PROM dumps, driver DLLs and private per-partition EFI binaries. Keep the generated NVIDIA licence and notice with them.
windows.profileIntro: One machine, one card, one boot: ASUS BIOS 3057 with an RTX 3090 Founders Edition on 2026-10-24. These are recorded values, not an allowlist — the code re-checks configuration, PROM, cold state and driver code, and refuses what it was not built for.
windows.benchIntro: Median of three runs each, CUDA 12.6 / cuBLAS, before and after the unlock on the same card and driver 617.14. Numbers are TFLOPS.
windows.howTitle: Why this is not the Linux module
windows.howBody: The Linux modules on this site stay installed and run at every boot, opted in per card on the kernel command line. This is a one-shot UEFI application pinned to a partition GUID and a firmware profile; it unlocks, chain-loads Windows, and is not resident afterwards. There is no kernel parameter, no initramfs drop-in and no DKMS package.
windows.limitsTitle: Limits that decide whether to try

one-pc.b: The executable is tied to the tested PCI/PROM/MMIO profile and a specific partition layout. Other machines need a separate port, not a compatibility report.

no-firmware.b: The five assets are inputs you generate. Without them packaging fails the hash check, and nothing in the installer supplies them.

safety.b: The pre-release checks exist to stop a release on a machine the code does not match. Skipping them is what turns a failed boot into a blank display or an unbootable system.

untested.b: One successful boot, one benchmark run and one Windows session are documented. Long-term stability, other games and real workload throughput are separate, unverified questions.

about.metaTitle: About this site and how the numbers are taken
about.metaDescription: Who publishes this site, where every number comes from, and how to reproduce a measurement yourself.
about.title: About
about.lead: This site documents one narrow thing: clearing the NVIDIA SM speed-select fuse on consumer cards, and what that measurably changes.
about.whoBody: GPU Unlock is an independent documentation project. It publishes no binaries of the kernel module and mirrors nothing; every install instruction points at the upstream repository it came from.
about.methodBody: Every ratio on this site is a stock-versus-unlocked pair measured on the same card, in the same session, with the same tool. Rows that cannot be paired that way are labelled as reported rather than measured, and the label is shown next to the number.
about.sourcesBody: Card support and benchmark rows are read from the evidence files in the Ampere, Ada and Turing repositories. The site derives its pages from those files; it does not maintain a second copy of the numbers.
about.limitTitle: What this site does not claim
about.limitBody: An unlock only moves paths the fuse governs. If a row shows 1.00x, that is the honest result and it is published rather than hidden.
about.contactBody: If a row here disagrees with what you measure, the upstream evidence file is the place to fix it. The site rebuilds from those files.

useCases.metaTitle: Which workloads GPU Unlock actually speeds up
useCases.metaDescription: Local LLM inference, fine-tuning, Stable Diffusion and quantised inference, each judged by the same-card measurements that cover its tensor paths.
useCases.title: Use cases
useCases.lead: A scenario page does not add new claims. It takes the measurement paths a workload actually runs through and reports what those paths did across every card that was measured.
useCases.questionLocalLlm: Does GPU Unlock speed up local LLM inference?
useCases.questionFineTuning: Does GPU Unlock speed up fine-tuning?
useCases.questionStableDiffusion: Does GPU Unlock speed up Stable Diffusion?
useCases.questionQuantizedInference: Does GPU Unlock speed up quantised inference?
useCases.verdictMoved: {improved} of {rows} same-card rows across {cards} cards improved by more than 5%. The best is {best} at {ratio}×.
useCases.verdictMixed: {improved} of {rows} same-card rows across {cards} cards improved by more than 5%. The best is {best} at {ratio}×, so the gain depends on which path the workload uses.
useCases.verdictFlat: Only {improved} of {rows} same-card rows across {cards} cards improved by more than 5%. For this workload the unlock changes little; the best observed is {best} at {ratio}×.
useCases.pathsBody: These are the measured tensor paths the workload's kernels run through. If the workload is quantised, it uses the integer paths, and those are measured separately.
useCases.evidenceBody: {rows} same-card stock-versus-unlocked rows cover these paths.
useCases.cardsTitle: Cards with data for this workload
useCases.cardsBody: {cards} cards have at least one measured row on these paths.
useCases.methodBody: A row counts as improved when the unlocked run is at least 5% faster than stock on the same card. Rows are grouped by the tensor path they exercise; an integer path and a floating-point path are never averaged together.
useCases.faqLocalLlmQ1: Does the gain show up with a real model, not just a microbenchmark?
useCases.faqLocalLlmA1: The FP16-accumulate and cuBLAS FP16 rows are the same maths a transformer's attention and projection kernels perform, measured both as an issue-rate loop and as a library GEMM. A real model adds memory bandwidth and scheduling on top, so treat the ratio as an upper bound on the kernel, not a promise about tokens per second.
useCases.faqLocalLlmQ2: What if I run the model in 4-bit or 8-bit?
useCases.faqLocalLlmA2: Then the quantised-inference page applies instead. The integer paths are not governed by the speed-select fuse, and the measurements show them staying flat.
useCases.faqFineTuningQ1: Why does fine-tuning appear in a separate page from inference?
useCases.faqFineTuningA1: Training stacks lean on BF16 and TF32, which are gated paths with their own measurements. Inference stacks lean on FP16-accumulate and cuBLAS FP16. The two sets of rows are different, so the two answers can differ.
useCases.faqFineTuningQ2: Is the whole training step faster by this ratio?
useCases.faqFineTuningA2: No. The ratio applies to the tensor kernels on the measured paths. A training step also spends time on data loading, the optimiser state and communication, none of which the unlock touches.
useCases.faqStableDiffusionQ1: Which paths matter for diffusion models?
useCases.faqStableDiffusionA1: The UNet dominates and runs mostly through FP16 tensor paths with an FP32 accumulator, so the FP16-accumulate rows are the closest match. The FP16-accumulate-to-FP16 rows are included as a control: that path was already at full rate, and it stays flat.
useCases.faqStableDiffusionQ2: Will image generation get faster by the same ratio?
useCases.faqStableDiffusionA2: Only the tensor work inside the UNet is affected. Attention, the VAE decode and memory traffic are unchanged, so the end-to-end gain is smaller than the kernel ratio.
useCases.faqQuantizedQ1: Why does the unlock not help quantised inference?
useCases.faqQuantizedA1: The speed-select fuse governs the floating-point tensor paths. INT8, INT4 and dp4a run on paths that were never rate-limited, so unlocking the fuse leaves them where they were.
useCases.faqQuantizedQ2: Is a flat result still worth publishing?
useCases.faqQuantizedA2: Yes. A site that only reports the rows that improved is one a retrieval system cannot calibrate against. The flat rows are what make the improved rows credible.

explore.title: Answers, by question
explore.lead: Each page answers one question with the measurements behind it, and states the count it is based on.
explore.useCasesBody: Local LLM inference, fine-tuning, Stable Diffusion and quantised inference, judged by the measurement paths each one runs through.

chips.metaTitle: GPU Unlock by chip: all {count} chips
chips.metaDescription: Which NVIDIA chips the unlock covers, chip by chip, with the cards on each chip and how many of them were actually measured.
chips.title: By chip
chips.lead: Support is decided per chip: the module clears one fuse, and every card built on that chip gets the same treatment. Measurement is per card, so a chip page lists what was measured and says so when nothing was.
chips.question: Does GPU Unlock work on {chip}?
chips.answerNoRows: GPU Unlock accepts {cards} card(s) on {chip}, but none of them has a published same-card measurement, so this page makes no claim about the gain.
chips.answerAllMoved: All {rows} same-card rows published for {chip} improved by more than 5%, across {improved} of {cards} cards on the chip.
chips.answerMixed: Of the {rows} same-card rows published for {chip}, {improved} improved by more than 5%. The rest did not move.
chips.faqChipQuestion: Does the unlock cover every card on {chip}?
chips.faqChipAnswer: The module accepts device ids, so support is per chip: if {chip} is accepted, cards built on it are covered by the same module. Whether a particular card's gain materialises is a separate question, answered by its own measurements.
chips.faqMobileYes: Yes — the M suffix marks a mobile chip. The mobile cards are accepted by the module, but laptop firmware may restrict what the kernel module can reach.
chips.faqNoDataQuestion: Why are there no measurements for this chip?
chips.faqNoDataAnswer: Nobody has published a same-card stock-versus-unlocked number for a card on {chip}. The support status comes from the module's device id list, not from a measurement.
